title: The Pot That Gave Birth
text:
Nasreddin Hodja borrowed a large cooking pot from his neighbor. A few days later he brought it back, and inside it sat a small pot.

The neighbor asked what the little pot was doing there. Congratulations, said Nasreddin. While your pot was at my house, it gave birth. Since the mother is yours, the child is yours too.

The neighbor thought this was nonsense, but he was not about to argue his way out of a free pot. He thanked Nasreddin warmly and took both pots inside.

Some time later Nasreddin came to borrow the big pot again. The neighbor lent it gladly, perhaps hoping for another little one. Days passed, then weeks, and the pot did not come back. At last the neighbor went to Nasreddin's house to ask for it.

Nasreddin looked very sad. I am sorry to tell you, he said, that your pot has died.

The neighbor was outraged. Died? How can a pot die? Who ever heard of such a thing?

Nasreddin shrugged. You believed it could give birth, he said. Why can you not believe it could die?
lesson: If you accept a convenient falsehood because it benefits you, you lose the right to object when the same logic turns against you. Hold to the same standard in gains and losses.
caveat: Nasreddin is a figure of folklore; stories attributed to him were collected and added over centuries.
